name: GETSTR
blurb: The $C2 GETSTR line-input opcode: prompts, reads a whole line with echo and backspace handling, then prints it back with PRINTSTR. GETSTR handles one character per execution and yields between them, so other VMs keep running while this one waits.

name: String Store
blurb: Storing strings for later: GETSTR reads three lines, $3B COPYMXMY block-copies each into a numbered 32-byte slot, and PRINTSTR reads them back out of order. Shows the slot pattern for keeping text around.

name: Prime-Gen v05
blurb: Odd-only trial division; prints primes 3 to 59. Exercises SERIN input, decimal parse, DIVXY + remainder test, decimal print.

name: Prime-Gen v07
blurb: Prime generator using the native OUTDEC opcode ($6E) for decimal print — CVT2DEC + OUTDEC, ~6x faster and smaller than the hand-rolled printer.

name: Prime-Gen v04
blurb: Earlier prime generator using a multiply-back divisibility test; primes 3 to 29.

name: Banner
blurb: Big-letter ASCII banner from a 5x5 pre-rendered font. Exercises indexed memory reads and nested loops.

name: Simple-Calc-5 (5 digits, bytecode)
blurb: A five-digit decimal calculator written entirely in STELLAR bytecode: 1/7 = 0.14286, 60000*60000 = 3600000000, 1/60000/60000 = 2.7778E-10. Works left to right like a pocket calculator (2+3*4 = 20); a line starting with + * / carries on from the last answer; a leading - is a negative number; 5/0 = Err. Numbers are a 16-bit mantissa and a decimal exponent, and every result is rounded, not truncated - all the arithmetic is native STELLAR ops (MULTXY, DIVXY, DIVMAX). Enter on its own quits. 2+3*4 is pre-typed; click the terminal to type more. Compare Simple-Calc-8, which does its arithmetic in native 1802 code. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Simple-Calc-8 (8 digits, RUNMC)
blurb: An eight-digit calculator: 1/7 = 0.14285714, 99999999*99999999 = 9.9999998E15. Works left to right (2+3*4 = 20); a line starting with + * / carries on from the last answer; a leading - is a negative number; Enter on its own quits. The arithmetic is native 1802 code called through RUNMC, on numbers held one decimal digit per byte, so every answer is correctly rounded to 8 digits. 1/7 is pre-typed; click the terminal to type more.

name: Pi digits
blurb: The digits of pi, worked out one at a time by the Rabinowitz-Wagon spigot - whole numbers only. Click the terminal, type how many digits (up to 1526; Enter alone = 100) and watch them come: 3. then groups of ten, fifty to a line. The digit logic is STELLAR bytecode; each pass over the array runs as raw 1802 code through RUNMC, with no multiply at all - 18x faster than the bytecode alone (compare 'Pi digits Stellar only'). On the Elf2K 100 digits take about 27 seconds, 1000 about half an hour. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Pi digits Stellar only
blurb: The same pi spigot as 'Pi digits', but every step is STELLAR bytecode - no native code. Type how many digits (up to 350; Enter alone = 50). It shows what the interpreter alone costs: on the Elf2K 100 digits take about 8 minutes here, against 27 seconds with the RUNMC inner loop.

name: ELIZA (chatbot)
blurb: The 1966 therapist chatbot. Runs flat out. Wait for WHAT'S YOUR NAME?, click the terminal, type your name, then talk to it in plain English - lower case is fine; BYE ends it. The text work (keyword search, pronoun swapping) is native 1802 code called through RUNMC, so replies start in a fraction of a second; it rotates its replies, remembers what you said after "my" and brings it back, and notices when you repeat yourself. Uses SETSIZE to take 12KB.

name: MOONBASE (text adventure)
blurb: A text adventure: a moonquake has wrecked the base and the air is running out - get to the lander and off the ground. Type one- or two-word commands (N, S, E, W, IN, OUT, LOOK, TAKE WRENCH, OPEN LOCKER, READ LOG, HELP...). Every game is shuffled: the moment you press the start key decides where things are, the airlock code and more. Click the terminal and press a key to begin. A native 1802 parser (RUNMC) reads each line; the game itself is STELLAR bytecode.

name: Lite-Writer 2 (word processor)
blurb: A full-screen word processor. Click the terminal and type: words wrap at column 72, and the status bar on line 24 shows the slot, line, column, bytes free and MODIFIED. Arrows move; Home/End, PgUp/PgDn and Delete work; Backspace and ^D delete; ^K cuts a line and ^U pastes it; ^F finds text; ^S and ^L save to and load from four slots; ^N starts a new document; ^G shows all the keys; ^X leaves. (On Windows and Linux the browser keeps Ctrl-N and Ctrl-T for itself.) The editor is STELLAR bytecode; a native 1802 engine called through RUNMC runs the terminal and the text buffer, and reads the keyboard while it writes to the screen, so no key is lost. Uses SETSIZE and VM4's memory. Verified on the Elf2K. Its four slots stay in memory when you load another program - so text left by Morse Receiver v11 opens here with ^L.

name: Tic-Tac-Toe
blurb: You are X, the computer is O. Click the terminal and type a square number 1-9 then Enter; empty squares show their numbers, so the board is its own legend. The computer wins if it can, blocks you if it must, and otherwise takes the centre, then a corner, then a side. One game per run - Reset to play again. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Mandelbrot
blurb: ASCII Mandelbrot, 40 x 24, in Q8.8 sign-magnitude fixed point. v09, rewritten for V0061.33: MULTXY + COPYAX MA make a multiply three opcodes, and the escape loop is all inline - 2.5x faster than the July version, with byte-identical output. Try 10x or flat out; at Elf2K speed it takes about 4½ minutes.

name: Front panel (Q + hex display)
blurb: Drives the Elf2K front panel instead of the terminal: lights the Q lamp and counts $00-$1F on the two-digit output display, then clears Q and halts. Serial output stays empty — watch the panel.

name: Morse Sender v18 (700 Hz tone - turn Sound on)
blurb: Sends what you type as Morse code on the Q line - every dot and dash a 700 Hz tone, made by a little raw-1802 loop run through RUNMC. Click 🔈 Sound under the Front Panel to hear it (the clock must be at Elf2K). The input box pre-loads 12 WPM and 'CQ DE STELLAR'; then click the terminal and type more lines. Speeds 5-25 WPM; Enter on an empty line quits. The pitch byte is at $4E42 (2A = 700 Hz; bigger = lower). For keying real Morse equipment use v17 (in the downloads), which holds Q steady. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Morse Receiver v11 (key INPUT, or 🎤 Listen)
blurb: Reads Morse from the INPUT switch (EF4) and learns the sender's speed as it goes. Click the terminal: choose a Lite-Writer 2 slot for the text (1-4, Enter = do not save), then a speed (Enter = 12). Key it by holding ⏺ INPUT under the Front Panel - or click 🎤 Listen and let it hear a 700 Hz tone: Morse Sender v18 with Sound on, on another computer. Keep the clock at Elf2K and the room quiet. Q or Esc quits; then load 'Lite-Writer 2' and press ^L and the slot number to edit what was received. Simulator-verified; not yet run on the Elf2K.

name: Starfield (VT100)
blurb: Stars streaming outward from the centre, the way they look from the front window of something moving fast. Each star just does ox += ox/4 every frame - no division, no multiplication, no signed arithmetic - and because both axes grow by the same factor every star travels a straight ray. Needs the VT100 terminal: it positions the cursor for every star. Type a count at the prompt, ESC stops it.

name: Bouncing Ball (VT100)
blurb: Two 3x3 reverse-video balls bouncing off the walls and off each other. Equal masses in an elastic collision exchange velocities, so the balls simply swap direction flags, and only the stale edge of each ball is erased, which keeps it flicker-free. v05 is 3.1x faster than v04: cursor digits come from lookup tables instead of DIVXY, and each ball is drawn with one cursor move and one PRINTSTR. Press a key to launch, ESC stops it.

name: Invaders (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Two rows of six invaders, an arrow-key gun and a rocket. Click the terminal and steer with the left and right arrows, space to fire; the aliens drop bombs back. Needs both the VT100 screen and the arrow keys, which the terminal now sends as the three-byte escape a real VT100 sends.

name: Pong (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: You are the paddle on the RIGHT; the computer plays the left. Click the terminal and press any key to serve, then steer with the up and down arrows (w and s work too). Where the ball strikes your paddle decides which way it leaves - top cell up, bottom cell down. First to 9 wins; Q quits. Opens at Elf2K speed - the real hardware's pace. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Racer (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Keep the car on the winding road. Click the terminal and press any key to start; the left and right arrows steer, up and down change the speed (1-9, shown bottom left with the distance), and a lone ESC quits. Touch either edge and you crash - any key drives again. The whole screen scrolls down with a plain VT100 reverse index (ESC M at the top line) - the one way of scrolling down Craig's terminal supports. Opens at Elf2K speed - the real hardware's pace. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Lunar Lander (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Bring the lander down gently on the '=' pad. Click the terminal and press E for Easy or H for Hard. The up arrow fires the main engine, left and right the side thrusters - one burst per press, each costing fuel (hold a key to repeat). Land with all three feet on the pad, falling slowly and hardly drifting. Easy has half the gravity, finer bursts, more fuel, a gentler limit and a wider pad. ESC quits; E or H flies again on a new random moon. Opens at Elf2K speed. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Snake (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Steer the snake to the food '*'. Click the terminal and press SPACE; the arrow keys (or w a s d) steer. Each food scores 1 and makes the snake 3 longer, and every 4 it gets faster (levels 0-9). Hit a wall or yourself and the game is over - SPACE plays again, P pauses, a lone ESC quits. The body is the grid itself: each cell remembers which way the snake left it, and the tail follows those arrows. Opens at Elf2K speed - the real hardware's pace. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Breakout (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Knock out the wall of bricks with the ball. Click the terminal and press SPACE; the arrow keys (or a / d) move the paddle. Reverse-video bricks score 5, '######' 3, '======' 1. Where the ball strikes the paddle sets its angle: the ends send it out wide, the middle steep. Three balls; each serve's first drop is slower so you can get there. Clear the wall and a faster one comes. P pauses, a lone ESC quits, SPACE plays again. Which brick the ball has reached is three table lookups - no divide. Opens at Elf2K speed - the real hardware's pace. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Tetris (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: Steer the falling pieces and clear the rows. Click the terminal and press SPACE (or a digit 0-9 to start at that level). Left / right arrows (or a / d) move the piece, up (or w) rotates it, z rotates it back, down (or s) moves it down a row, SPACE drops it. 1-4 rows at once score 10 / 30 / 50 / 80 points times the level + 1; every 10 rows the level goes up and the pieces fall faster. P pauses, ESC quits. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Galaxia (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: A Galaxian-style shooter. Click the terminal and press any key. Left / right arrows (or z / x) move your ship, SPACE fires - keys are queued while the screen is drawn, so a held arrow keeps moving. The swarm sways overhead: flagships 60, reds 50, purples 40, blues 30. Divers swoop down, chase you and drop bombs - shoot one in flight for double points. Three ships; each wave dives more often. P pauses, R restarts, Q quits. Stellar C with a native frame engine. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Battleship (VT100, arrow keys)
blurb: You against the computer on two 10 x 10 seas: carrier 5, battleship 4, cruiser 3, submarine 3, destroyer 2. Click the terminal and press SPACE; R shuffles your fleet, SPACE starts the battle. The arrow keys move your aim over ENEMY WATERS and SPACE or Enter fires - or type a square (B7, J10) to jump there. The computer hunts on a checkerboard and works round every hit. Q gives up and shows its ships. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: CanonBall (VT100, you vs the computer)
blurb: Your castle and great cannon on the left, the computer's on the right. Click the terminal and choose 1 Easy, 2 Normal or 3 Hard. Up / Down arrows (or W / S) raise and lower your barrel a degree at a time; SPACE fires. The ball flies in a real arc and leaves a trail of dots to aim by; the wind, different every game, pushes every ball. Then the computer fires back - it watches where its last ball came down and corrects. The first castle knocked down loses. Written in Stellar C. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: CanonBall Solo (VT100, target practice)
blurb: Knock down the castle across the field in as few shots as you can. Click the terminal and press SPACE; Up / Down arrows (or W / S) aim the barrel, SPACE fires, and the last shot's trail of dots shows where you went wrong. A hit knocks bricks off five columns; the castle falls when three quarters of it is gone. Written in Stellar C. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Getting Warmer (guess the number)
blurb: The computer picks a number from 1 to 1000 and you have ten guesses. Click the terminal, press any key, then type a guess and Enter. Each answer says go higher or lower - and from the second guess on whether you are getting warmer or colder than your last one. Ten is always enough if you halve the range each time. A line that is not a number from 1 to 1000 costs nothing; Q gives up; Y plays again, N quits. Plain text: no VT100 needed. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Big Clock (VT100: chime, alarm, timer)
blurb: The time in big seven-segment digits made of reverse-video blocks, with the day of the week and the date underneath - plus a timer, an hourly chime that strikes the hour and an alarm with snooze, both sounding on Q (click 🔈 Sound under the Front Panel to hear them). On the Elf2K it reads the DS12887 real-time clock through the $07 RTC opcode; here the simulator's clock chip runs on this computer's own clock. Click the terminal: T starts a timer and T again stops it, showing the time passed; C turns the chime on or off, A sets the alarm (HH:MM, Enter = off), S sets the clock, Q quits. When the alarm rings, Z snoozes 9 minutes and any other key stops it. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Starship (VT100)
blurb: The COSMAC ELF logo with its STELLAR EDITION caption, stored as a run table - line, first column, length - rather than a bitmap. 108 runs paint the whole picture. Any key clears it.

name: Game of Life (VT100)
blurb: Conway's Game of Life on a 40x20 grid, seeded with a blinker and a glider.

name: Life Lab (VT100: draw your own Game of Life)
blurb: Conway's Game of Life that you seed yourself. Click the terminal and press any key. EDIT: the arrow keys (or W A S D) move the cursor, SPACE turns a cell on or off, 1-9 stamp a pattern at the cursor (1 glider, 2 spaceship, 3 R-pentomino, 4 acorn, 5 glider gun, 6 pulsar, 7 diehard, 8 ten in a row, 9 infinite growth), C clears, R fills the board at random, T steps one generation. ENTER runs it; SPACE or ENTER stops and goes back to editing with the board kept; + and - change the speed. The 78 x 20 board wraps round. Written in Stellar C, with the generation in native 1802 code. Verified on the Elf2K.

name: Sort visualiser (VT100)
blurb: Watch STELLAR's $FC PULSESORTXY opcode sort twenty numbers. Each pass is ONE opcode - one bubble-sort pass - and only the bars that moved are redrawn; it stops when a pass finds nothing to swap. Click the terminal and press any key to start; when sorted, A sorts up, D sorts down, N gives new numbers, Q quits. Runs at the Elf2K's own speed.
